key_insight: General forgetting-mitigation methods that look effective on broad benchmarks do not necessarily preserve machine-translation-specific instruction following. In other words, fixing catastrophic forgetting for translation fine-tuning is not the same as preserving controllable translation behavior like formality, gender, or length.
problem_solved: The paper addresses catastrophic forgetting during LLM fine-tuning on parallel translation data, especially whether standard mitigation methods also preserve MT-specific instruction following (MT-IF) such as style, grammatical gender, and length control.
method: Fine-tune LLMs on parallel data for translation and evaluate forgetting.
Compare mitigation strategies anchored to auxiliary data, model outputs, and other retention signals.
Measure not only general benchmark retention, but also MT-specific instruction following after fine-tuning.
impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this shows that translation systems need evaluation beyond generic forgetting benchmarks. If your application depends on controllable translation, you must test whether mitigation methods preserve those translation-specific behaviors, not just overall model knowledge.
visual_elements: Before/after pipeline showing pretraining -> translation fine-tuning -> forgetting mitigation -> evaluation on MT-IF
Side-by-side score cards for general benchmark retention vs MT-specific instruction following
Icon set for translation controls: formality, gender, and length
Comparison chart of different mitigation methods and their effects on translation quality and MT-IF
paper_title: Fine-Tuning LLMs for Translation: General Forgetting Mitigation Does Not Preserve MT-Specific Instruction Following
paper_authors: Niklas Scholz, David Thulke, Abdallah Nasir, Will Allred, Evgeny Matusov
